activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: Many proportional systems set a minimum vote share for winning seats; in Germany a party usually needs at least 5 percent of the national party vote, with limited exceptions.
story:
Ava had never been inside a courthouse before, and the marble hallway made her sneakers squeak in a way she was sure the whole county could hear. Her class was there for a mock election demonstration, part of Mr. Khan's civics project, and rows of folding chairs faced a long table where the vote counts would be tallied. She clutched her worksheet, which listed six pretend parties and their vote totals, and felt the first rumble of a problem: Mr. Khan had promised that whoever made the clearest argument about the results would get to present them to the visiting eighth graders, and Tatum wanted the job just as badly as she did.

The exercise was tedious at first, adding column after column of sample votes, and Ava kept losing her place. "First-past-the-post was easier," Tatum whispered, jabbing at the paper. "Most votes wins, done." Under that column, the Blue Party had won every seat in the mock district even though only 41 percent of voters picked it. Ava stared at that number. Something was hiding underneath the arithmetic, a pattern she couldn't see yet, and it made the back of her neck prickle.

She flipped to the second column, where the seats were handed out in proportion to each party's share of the vote, and started testing an idea. The Green Party had 3 percent. If votes translated straight into seats, three out of every hundred belonged to Green voters, so a small party should flourish under this system, not vanish the way it had under first-past-the-post. But when she reached for the seat chart, she found the Green row blank. She counted again, then a third time. Three percent, no seats.

"That's not fair," said Kaylie, leaning over from the next row of chairs. "They got real votes. Somebody voted for them." Ava said the same thing, but even as she said it, she was thinking about the blank row. Maybe it wasn't a mistake. Maybe there was a rule underneath, invisible in the vote totals but doing real work.

When Mr. Khan called for observations, Tatum went first and argued that the Greens deserved a seat. Ava raised her hand. "I checked, and it's not an error," she said, standing up in the squeaky hallway silence. "Many proportional systems set a minimum vote share for winning seats. In Germany, a party usually needs at least 5 percent of the national party vote, with limited exceptions. Our Greens got 3 percent, so under that rule they'd get nothing." Mr. Khan asked where she'd found it, and she held up her phone, showing the page she'd pulled from an elections database in the courthouse's slow public wifi.

Tatum stared at the blank Green row for a long moment, then shut his worksheet. "I wanted them to get a seat because it felt fair," he admitted. "But the rule is the rule, and honestly, a threshold like that probably keeps a hundred tiny parties from crowding the chamber." Kaylie still frowned, but she copied Ava's citation onto her own sheet. Mr. Khan wrote two names on the sign-up sheet for the presentation, side by side, and Ava slid her worksheet across the table toward Tatum. "You take first-past-the-post," she said. "I'll take the rest."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Sweat cools the body as it evaporates, so in humid weather, when sweat evaporates slowly, athletes cool down less well and overheat more easily.
story:
The gym at the community center smelled like rubber and old popcorn, but the real problem was the air itself, thick as soup, because someone had propped the doors open and let the August evening pour in. Lillian jogged to midcourt for warmups and already felt her shirt sticking to her back. Kolten fanned himself with a cone from the water station and groaned, "It's only eighty degrees. Why do I feel like I ran a marathon?"

By halftime, the whole team was dragging. Charles-Edouard, who usually sprinted for every loose ball, stood with his hands on his knees, and even the sub bench was silent. Lillian looked down at her arms. Sweat was beading on her skin and just sitting there, dripping off her elbow instead of drying. She turned it over in her mind while Mr. Pierre called a play she barely heard. Last Saturday had been hotter, ninety-five at least, but the air had been dry, and everyone had played hard right to the final whistle. So the heat itself couldn't be the thing that wrecked them.

"You're staring at your arm," Kolten said during a water break.

"My sweat isn't drying," she said. "Watch." She held her forearm out, and a bead of moisture slid slowly toward her wrist and dropped. "Saturday it dried fast, and I felt fine."

Charles-Edouard shrugged. "So we sweat more today."

"No, we sweat the same amount, maybe more. It just sits there." She remembered a poster from science class, something about evaporation, and the pieces clicked quietly into place. "Sweat only cools you when it dries off you. Today the air's already soaked, so it dries slow, and we can't cool down."

Mr. Pierre overheard and gave her a look she couldn't read, half skeptical, half something else. "You saying my gym's broken?"

"I'm saying we need to close the doors and get the fans on the players, not the ball rack." Her voice came out more defiant than she meant, and she braced for him to bench her. He had benched her once last season, for arguing about a call, and she'd sat the whole fourth quarter replaying it, wondering if she should have stayed quiet.

Instead he squinted at the propped doors, then at his gasping team. "Kolten, Charles-Edouard, shut them. Move the fans here." Then, quieter, to Lillian: "You should have said that at the start of the half."

She thought of the first two quarters, the team wilting while she said nothing, and didn't have an answer for that yet. The doors clanged shut. The big floor fans hummed to life, and Kolten stood in front of one with his arms spread like he was trying to salvage the whole game from the breeze alone. By the fourth quarter the air still hung heavy, but the sweat on Lillian's neck began to dry at last, prickling cold, and her legs felt like hers again. She stole a pass at the top of the key and drove.

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: An ad hominem argument attacks the person making a claim instead of the claim itself, and it is counted as a fallacy, a flaw in reasoning.
story:
Jonathan had come to drama camp to audition for the villain in the camp play, so when Mr. Rajapakse announced that Friday would be a debate showcase instead, it felt like being handed a script for the wrong movie. "Same skill," Mr. Rajapakse said, pacing the stage. "A character wants something and argues for it. You'll build a case: a claim, evidence, and a warrant for each point, by Thursday." Thursday. Jonathan wrote the deadline on his hand in blue pen, then circled it twice, because circled things felt more official.

He spread his notes across the piano bench in the prop room, where cardboard swords leaned against the wall like a symmetrical forest. His claim was ready: the camp should move its showcase to the outdoor stage. His evidence was strong: forty more seats, better acoustics, no rental fee for the gym. But the warrant, the reason the evidence proved the claim, kept sliding away from him like a dropped prop rolling under the bleachers. His friend Rayan flopped onto a beanbag and narrated Jonathan's struggle like a sports announcer: "He reaches for the warrant. He stretches. He misses it entirely."

Then Tuesday happened. Tiana, arguing the other side, got up in practice and said, "Why should we listen to Jonathan? He's only here because he flubbed his audition for the villain." A few people laughed. Jonathan felt his face go hot, and he almost fired back about her squeaky stage whisper. Instead he grabbed the yellow debate handbook from the prop shelf and flipped through it until he found the entry. He read it once, then twice, and something clicked into place like the final piece of a puzzle box.

That night he wrote a note and left it in Tiana's cubby before lights-out.

"Tiana, you attacked me, not my argument, and the book says that's a fallacy called ad hominem. Judges mark it down. So you did me a favor. Tomorrow, argue the gym is better because the outdoor stage floods and the mosquitoes eat the audience. Attack the claim. I'll be ready. Jonathan."

At the Thursday showcase, Tiana followed the note. Her case about flooding was so good that Jonathan had to use his warrant out loud for the first time: "More seats matter because a showcase is for the audience, so the venue that fits the most people serves the purpose best." Mr. Rajapakse's pencil paused over his scoring sheet. Afterward he tapped the paper and said, "That, and the moment you didn't hit back when she went after you. That's the round." Rayan hoisted Jonathan onto his shoulders and marched him toward the cardboard swords, shouting, "The outdoor stage claims its champion!"

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: Box breathing means breathing in for a count of four, holding for four, breathing out for four and holding for four, then repeating the pattern.
story:
Michael's hands were shaking again, and he couldn't figure out why. Nothing scary was happening. He was just sitting at the kitchen table with his social studies project, three days before he had to present it in front of the whole class. His heart was drumming like it did before a race, except he hadn't moved in an hour. "Maybe I'm coming down with something," he told his mother, who felt his forehead and found nothing. He lay awake that night anyway, staring at the ceiling and listening to the refrigerator hum.

The next morning his friend Inara was at his house working on her own project. When Michael dropped his note cards for the third time, she paused. "You do this before every presentation," she said. "Last month too, with the science fair. Your hands, I mean." Michael stared at the scattered cards. Three presentations, three shaky weeks, three nights of barely sleeping. It wasn't a virus, and it wasn't bad luck. There was a pattern, and the pattern was him.

"It's stress," Inara said. "My cousin gets it before auditions. She taught me a thing she calls box breathing." Michael frowned. "What's a box got to do with breathing?" Inara tapped the kitchen table. "Watch. You breathe in for a count of four, then hold for four, breathe out for four, hold for four, and start again." She traced a square on the table, one side for each count, her finger moving slowly around the shape. "That's why it's called a box. Four sides, four counts."

Michael didn't believe a finger on a table could do anything. But that was a testable idea, and he liked testable ideas. He set a timer for two minutes and traced the square: in, hold, out, hold. His mind wandered twice, and he lost count, so he started over. The first minute felt silly. Somewhere in the second minute, he noticed his shoulders had dropped an inch, and the drumming in his chest had slowed to something more like tapping. He hadn't done anything to make that happen. The breathing had.

He practised all weekend. At night, instead of lying in the dark and letting the presentation replay over and over, he tried a routine: screens off at nine, the square traced on his pillow until his arms felt heavy, then lights out. Saturday he slept six hours. Sunday, eight. On Monday morning his neighbour Mr. Balogun waved from his porch as Michael left for school. "You look better than last week," Mr. Balogun said. "Less grey around the gills." Michael laughed. It wasn't a permanent fix, and it wouldn't permit him to skip the nerves entirely, but it was something he could actually carry in his pocket.

Standing beside the projector with his cue cards, Michael felt the familiar drumming start. He put one finger low on the desk, where nobody could see, and drew the first side of a square. In. Hold. Out. Hold. He looked up at Mr. Balogun's empty chair, then at Inara, who raised her eyebrows and traced a tiny square right back at him on her desk. "Okay," Michael said. "My project is on the water cycle."

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: Ohm's law is named after the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm, who published it in 1827.
story:
Sophie knelt on the cold garage floor between two cardboard boxes, a battery, a tangled multimeter, and a lamp that would never light again. "It's dead," she said, holding up the bulb, its filament snapped like a burnt hair. Walid crouched beside her, chewing a carrot, because he ate like a herbivore at every snack break and this one was no exception. "It died for science," he said. Sophie didn't laugh. She had grabbed the thin spool of wire without checking it first, an impulsive move, and the bulb had paid the price.

The plan had been simple: build a headlamp for the old wagon they were restoring in the garage. Now she had two mystery spools, thick and thin, and no idea which one had cooked the bulb. She couldn't see inside the copper to find out, so she decided to test it the way Ms. Farah had shown them in class, with numbers instead of eyes. She clipped the thick spool into a circuit with a fresh battery, read 6 volts on the meter, then broke the circuit and measured the current. She wrote both numbers on the dusty workbench with her finger to remember them, then divided voltage by current on paper.

"Two ohms," she announced. She did the same with the thin spool and got nearly twelve. The thin wire was the killer. She had guessed it, but now she had proof she could show, and proof could be conveyed to anyone, even to Walid's little brother who insisted nothing in the garage was dangerous.

"Ohms," Walid repeated, leaning over her shoulder. "Weird word. Why is it called that?" Sophie said she didn't know, but the question stuck in her head like a burr. She dug through the box of her uncle's old textbooks on the shelf by the paint cans, sneezing twice, until she found a thin blue one with a cracked spine. She flipped pages by the garage door's gray light. There it was, in faded print: the unit was named after Georg Simon Ohm, a German physicist, who had published the law in 1827.

"Almost two hundred years ago," she said, "some German physicist did this same math, and now we say his name every time." She turned back to the bench, proud, and picked up the good spool to cut a length for the new lamp. The scissors went snip, and Walid said, "You just cut the piece we measured." Sophie looked down at the short curled length of proof in her hand, the only piece of thick wire left.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Across many sports, home teams win more than half their games on average, an effect known as home advantage.
story:
Romy's volleyball team had lost every away game since October, and she was tired of pretending it didn't bother her. What confused her was that the same team, the same passes, the same serves, looked completely different at the community center gym. There they had beaten Riverside in two straight sets, then rolled over Northgate, then won again on Thursday night, a scrappy three-setter against a team that had crushed them on the road 25-12. Romy lay on her bedroom floor afterward, bouncing a ball off the ceiling, trying to digest the idea that the losses and the wins were coming from the same twelve players.

"It can't be the gym," she told Mckinley at practice, spinning a ball on one finger. "A court is a court." McKinley, who kept the scorebook, flipped backward through the pages. Away games: zero wins. Home games: three. "Maybe it's not trivial," Romy said slowly. "Maybe it's a pattern." She grabbed a scrap of paper and went around the community center, asking the Saturday basketball league and the indoor soccer teams one question: how do you do at home versus away? The basketball coach shrugged and said they were about even, maybe a little better at home. The soccer captain said the same thing, better than even, but nobody could say why.

Myla, meanwhile, had her own problem. She wanted to audition for setter, but the coach kept her at libero, saying she was too short to see over the net. Myla practiced sets against the wall every day after warm-ups, fifty in a row, jaw set, until her forearms were pink. "You should just ask for the audition," Romy told her. "Worst thing she says is no." "Worst thing she says is no in front of everybody," Myla said, and served a ball into the bleachers by accident, which made them both laugh so hard Ms. Tremblay, who ran the center, came over to see what was wrong.

The next home game, Romy tested her idea. She played the first set the way she always did, and they won easily. In the second set, she deliberately pretended they were on the road, calling away-game warmups, using the visitors' bench. They lost 25-19. In the third set she gave it up and leaned into the home crowd instead, pointing to Myla after every good dig, and they won the match. Afterward McKinley found something in the community center library, a battered sports book, and read aloud that across many sports, home teams win more than half their games on average. "They call it home advantage," McKinley said. Romy grinned. Half didn't sound like much until you counted it over a whole season of everybody's games.

At the last practice of the season, Myla finally raised her hand and asked for her audition. The coach put her at setter for the full scrimmage, and Myla ran the offense like she'd been born there, dumping a sneaky second-touch over the net that fooled even Romy. "That," Ms. Tremblay called from the doorway, "is why I never close this gym early."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages, so something posted publicly can turn up in search results.
story:
George settled into the lobby of Skyfall Arena, headphones on, waiting for the match to fill. He was thirteen minutes early because Paige had messaged him that something weird was happening, and Paige was never weird about a game.

"You see this guy?" Paige typed in the team chat. A player named Vex_444 had joined, and the moment he did, he said: "George, right? Grade eight? You live near the river bridge."

George's fingers went still on the keyboard. His tag in the game was just FallenKite. It said nothing about his grade or his street. He typed back, "lol who's this," and Vex_444 answered with the name of his school and the words "heard you broke your nose at the skate park. Cartilage stuff, rough."

The match started and George played badly, missing shots he never missed, because he kept scrolling back up through the chat. His nose had healed months ago, and he had only told that story to his friends in the lobby, one late night in June. Paige, Lilianne, a couple of others. Nobody else.

After the match he quit to the menu and opened a browser beside the game. He had learned something in Ms. McKenzie's class weeks ago, half-listening, half-drawing: search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages, so anything posted publicly can turn up in search results. He remembered it now with a cold, specific feeling, because Vex_444 hadn't guessed anything. Vex_444 had read something.

He typed his own name into the search bar, held his breath, and hit enter. The third result was a forum thread titled "funniest lobby chat ever." It was a screenshot. His screenshot, his words, his skate park story in full, posted by an account that had copied the whole conversation from a public lobby archive and pasted it where anyone could find it. Anyone, including a stranger who wanted to act like a friend.

He tested it the only way he could think of. He went back to the lobby, created a second account with a different name, and typed a made-up detail into the chat: "anyone else going to the maroon warehouse Friday?" He logged off, waited an hour doing his homework badly, then searched the phrase. There it was, already in the results, copied and indexed from the public page. His made-up detail, sitting where any stranger could read it.

He wrote to Lilianne first, then Paige, in a group message: don't say anything real in public lobbies, everything gets copied. Then he reported Vex_444, blocked him, and typed one last line into the lobby before closing it, not to the stranger but to whoever else was quietly reading and pretending to be nobody.

"Nice try," George typed. "The warehouse isn't real."

The reply came back in three seconds: "I know. I've known everything else, though."

George stared at the screen, then reached over and pulled the ethernet cable from the wall.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A standard modern piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
story:
Andrew counted the keys on Mr. Brown's piano for the third time that Tuesday, and every time the number came out wrong in a different way.

"Fifty-two white," he muttered, running his finger along the row. "And the blacks keep moving on me."

"They don't migrate, Andrew," said Warren from the bench, where he was pretending to practice a scale. "They're just small. You skip them when you count fast."

Andrew wanted to know the exact number of keys because of a bet. Beatrix had claimed at lunch that every proper piano had 88 keys, exactly, no matter what. Andrew had said no piano company would build them all the same, because that would be boring. The loser had to carry the winner's trumpet case for a whole week, and Beatrix's trumpet case weighed about as much as a small dog, so the stakes were serious.

At his lesson, he told Mr. Brown he needed to check something before they started. Mr. Brown folded his arms and said he had five minutes, because Czerny waited for no man. Andrew counted the white keys one at a time, touching each with a fingertip so his eyes couldn't trick him. Fifty-two. Then he counted the black keys, which were worse because they sat in little groups with gaps between them, like teeth missing on a comb. Thirty-six. He added the numbers twice in his head. Eighty-eight.

"There's a trick to it," Warren said, watching from the corner. "The black keys come in twos and threes, all the way up. If you count the groups instead of the keys, you don't lose your place."

That was the logic Andrew had been missing. He counted again, tapping each group of two, then each group of three, all the way from the bottom of the keyboard to the top. The pattern held the whole way, stubborn and obstinate, refusing to break even once. He liked that about it. His own fingers were never that reliable.

"So it's really 88," Andrew said.

"It is," said Mr. Brown. "Fifty-two white and thirty-six black, on every standard modern piano you'll meet. Now, hands together, and don't let those black keys scare you. They're only small."

Andrew played his C major scale, hit a B-flat instead of a B, and decided the black keys were scary anyway, whatever Mr. Brown said.

The next day he found Beatrix at her locker and told her the count. She held out her hand, and he shook it, because a bet was a bet. Then she swung her trumpet case onto his shoulder, and it was exactly as heavy as advertised.

"Wait," Andrew said, shifting the case to the other shoulder. "Whose piano did you even count? You don't have one."

"My grandma's. I counted hers twice on Sunday." Beatrix smiled and walked off down the hall. "Fifty-two white, thirty-six black. Grandma says she'll lend it to you if you ever get good enough."

Andrew carried the case to the bus, counted the black keys in his head one more time out of pure habit, and got 36 again.

"Fine," he told the case. "You win."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In 1997, Major League Baseball retired Jackie Robinson's number 42 for every team, the first time any professional athlete was honored that way.
story:
Alexandre scanned the visiting team's lineup as they took the field, counting jersey numbers out of habit. His little sister pointed at the scoreboard and asked why nobody on either team wore 42, and he opened his mouth to answer before realizing he had no answer. "Maybe it's unlucky," he said. Mackenna, two seats over with a bucket of popcorn balanced on her knees, shook her head. "They wear 13 and everything. Try again."

The stadium was packed, the field a lush green stripe under the lights, and between pitches the four screens around the upper deck flashed old photographs in black and white. Alexandre stopped counting the players and started counting the photos. A man sliding into base. The same man shaking hands with teammates. The same man again, and in every single shot the same detail: a 42 on his jersey. "Look at that," he said, nudging Mackenna. "Every picture, number 42. That's not a coincidence."

Mackenna squinted at the screen. "So what? Old teams had old numbers." Alexandre disagreed, and he said so. He reasoned it out loud, fast, because the inning was moving. "If 42 was just old, then some player would wear it now. Numbers get reused. Nobody on either roster has it, and my sister noticed it before I did. It's not reuse. It's blocked. Something happened to that number." To test it, he pulled up the rosters on his phone and checked both teams, top to bottom, every pitcher in the bullpen. Forty-one, forty-three, every number around it, but never forty-two. "It's retired," he said. "Like, for everybody."

"Retired how?" Mackenna asked. Right then the giant screen changed. A message rolled across it in white letters, the same one, Alexandre guessed, that stadiums everywhere showed on this day: a tribute marking that in 1997, Major League Baseball retired Jackie Robinson's number 42 for every team, the first time any professional athlete was honored that way. The whole crowd stood up. So did Alexandre, still holding his phone with the rosters open.

"That's the guy from the photos," his sister said, tugging his sleeve. Alexandre nodded. He had guessed the mechanism right, one component of it anyway, the blocked number, though he had gotten the reason completely wrong. He had thought it was superstition, like a cursed number teams avoided. Instead a whole league had chosen to lock it away on purpose, everywhere at once, and nobody had needed to tell him for him to find it.

Ms. Villanueva, his old teacher from down the street, was in the next section and waved at them across the aisle. Mackenna cupped her hands and shouted over the noise, "Alexandre figured out the 42 thing before they announced it!" Alexandre sat back down, ears burning, and closed the roster page. On the field the next batter stepped in, wearing 24, and Alexandre's sister read the number out loud to nobody in particular.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: North of the Arctic Circle, the Sun stays up for at least one full day around the June solstice, which is called the midnight sun.
story:
Grayson had one weekend to figure out the seasons before Monday's retest, and he was doing it at his grandpa's house because his own kitchen table was buried under his little sister's art project. Ms. Weiss had written on his quiz, "You keep saying summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun. Show me you understand the tilt." He spread his notes on the kitchen table, then texted Mohamed-Amine and Harmony so he wouldn't feel like he was studying alone.

Grandpa set a mug of cocoa beside him and left him to it, humming from behind his newspaper. On his phone, Harmony sent a photo of a postcard her uncle had mailed from a trip north of the Arctic Circle, along with a message: "He says this was taken at MIDNIGHT. Look at the sun. It never set the whole time he was there. Isn't that wild?" In the picture, a low orange sun hung over a line of dark pines, lighting the water like late afternoon. Grayson squinted at it. If the sun was up at midnight, and this was around the June solstice, then something about that place made daylight refuse to end.

He grabbed the flashlight from the junk drawer and an orange from the bowl on the counter. He pushed a pencil through the orange to be the axis and tilted it, the way his textbook diagram showed, then shone the flashlight straight across the table like sunlight. The tilt meant the top half caught light at a steeper angle while the bottom half slanted away into shadow. He spun the orange slowly. The lit half stayed lit. That was the pattern, hidden because nobody could actually watch the whole planet at once; you had to build a small one.

"Midnight sun," Harmony typed when he asked her if there was a word for it. "That's what he says it's called." He whispered the words to himself, grinning, and noticed something else: the two halves of his orange looked almost the same in shape, but they weren't, not really. One leaned in, one leaned out, and if you ignored the tilt you'd destroy the whole symmetry of summer and winter trading places. That was where he had gone wrong on the quiz. He'd assumed "closer" because the real cause was invisible and his guess felt satisfying.

Mohamed-Amine messaged a question about distance, and Grayson started to type "closer means hotter" out of habit. He stopped, deleted it, and wrote instead, "Distance is ambiguous, it sounds right but it isn't the reason. The tilt is." It felt strange to type a correction to his own brain, but good strange, like catching a door before it slams.

Grandpa peered over his shoulder at the orange and the flashlight and the postcard photo. "So that thing tells you why January freezes my birdbath?"

"Basically," Grayson said, and spun the orange one more time, watching the shadow sweep across it like a slow hand.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: A settler's diary shows one person's view; it rarely tells how the Native American nations whose lands the trails crossed saw the same events.
story:
Levi had exactly one thing written on his notepad: "Why people moved west in the 1800s" and, underlined twice, "due tomorrow." He had put off the assignment all week, which was why he was now sitting in the public library at a table under a flickering light, next to Blake, who was supposedly helping but was mostly drawing a shark wearing a top hat.

"Ms. Szabó said we need a primary source," Levi said. "Not a textbook. Something from an actual person."

"Like a diary?" Blake said, not looking up from the shark.

Levi typed it into the library catalog and found a whole shelf of reproduced settler diaries, letters, and trail journals. He carried back a stack the height of a sandwich and started skimming. One diary, kept by a woman named Hannah who walked a wagon trail in the 1850s, was perfect. She wrote about bad soil back home, a sick brother who needed drier air, and a letter from her uncle claiming the land out west was cheap and the soil was rich. Levi copied three quotes, feeling like a detective. Case closed.

Then he reread one line: "We have seen no one for days, praise be, the land lies empty and waiting for us." Levi frowned. He knew from class that the land was not empty. Whole nations lived along those trails. He turned to Blake. "Here's the weird part. Hannah's diary is my primary source, and it's real, but it shows one person's view. It never tells how the Native American nations whose lands the trails crossed saw the same events."

"So use two sources," Blake said, finally capping his pen. "Assess the situation like a detective. Detectives get two witnesses."

Levi went back to the catalog and searched, feeling slightly desperate, since the report was due tomorrow and the library closed in an hour. He found a collection of recorded accounts from Native writers and elders describing the same trails, the same years. In one, a man remembered the wagons cutting through the grass and the rivers fouled where the herds crossed. Levi wrote both views side by side, and for the first time all week the assignment felt like something true instead of something finished.

At the checkout desk, the librarian squinted at his pile. "School project?" Levi nodded. "My heritage project too, sort of," he said. "My great-great-something actually walked one of those trails. Endangered species of assignment, though. One diary almost ate it." She laughed and stamped the due dates.

Levi's paper got read out loud in class. Ms. Szabó said, "This is how you use a primary source, and this is how you question one." Blake leaned over from the next desk and whispered, "I want top hat shark credit."

"Fine," Levi whispered back. "Footnote two: shark,Blake, one."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: The first call from a handheld cellular phone was made by Motorola engineer Martin Cooper on a New York street on April 3, 1973.
story:
The phone box sat on the kitchen table between Alexia's cereal bowl and her dad's coffee mug, and she could not stop staring at it. "After breakfast," he kept saying, but she had finished her toast in record time and was now spinning her spoon like a propeller. "I want to set it up before Henrik and Ricky come over. They've had phones for a year, and I don't want to look like a total beginner." Her dad laughed and slid the box across the table.

Inside, the phone was dark blue with a case that felt almost elastic, stretchy enough that she could peel it back at the corner and snap it into place again. "First rule," her dad said, holding up the charging cable. "It lives on the kitchen table overnight. Not in your room." Alexia rolled her eyes, but she plugged it in anyway, watching the battery icon fill like a thermometer on a warm day.

The doorbell rang twice before she got there, because she was reading the manual. Henrik and Ricky burst in with their own phones out, already arguing. "Phones have been around forever," Ricky said. "Like, decades." "No way," Henrik said. "Pocket phones are new. I bet they didn't exist when Ms. Tan was a kid."

Alexia set her phone down on the table like a judge's gavel. "We can settle this. We can ask Ms. Tan, she's right next door, and she knows everything about history." The three of them tore outside, and Ms. Tan was watering her roses like she had been waiting for them. When Alexia asked, Ms. Tan grinned. "Actually, I know this exactly. The first call from a handheld cellular phone was made by Motorola engineer Martin Cooper on a New York street on April 3, 1973." She counted off each part on her fingers. "A handheld phone. On a street. In 1973."

"Nineteen seventy-three," Ricky repeated, and Henrik tried to replicate the moment, holding an imaginary phone to his ear and marching around the garden path shouting "Hello? Hello? It's 1973!" Ms. Tan said Cooper had called a rival engineer, which made it even better, like scoring a goal in the other team's net.

Back at the kitchen table, Alexia made her very first call, to her grandmother, who answered on the second ring. "I did it," Alexia said. "It's me, from my own phone, at my own kitchen table." Her grandmother laughed so loudly that Henrik and Ricky could hear it across the room, and Alexia beamed down at the dark blue screen glowing in her hand.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: A eulogy is a speech praising a person who has died; the word comes from Greek roots meaning to 'speak well of'.
story:
Henry stood at the edge of the cemetery with a folded index card in his pocket and no idea what was written on it, because he had rewritten it six times and the last version just said PICK ONE MEMORY. His grandfather had kept bees behind the garage for forty years, and everyone expected Henry to speak at the service. Ms. Mansour, who had been his grandfather's neighbor, had asked him gently the day before. "A eulogy," she'd said, "just means a speech speaking well of someone who has died. It comes from Greek roots. Nobody expects a masterpiece." Henry had nodded, but the word had stuck in his head anyway. Speak well of. That was the whole job.

Caius and Lindsay found him near the fence, where gray lichen spread over the stones like slow spilled paint. "Did you pick a memory?" Caius asked. Henry shook his head. "I keep thinking they all need to be in there. The bees, the card games, the time he drove two hours in the rain for my soccer game. But Ms. Mansour said a eulogy is only about speaking well of him, not saying everything about him." Lindsay frowned. "So it's like a highlight, not a biography." Henry had not thought of it that way, and the idea loosened something in his chest.

He decided to test it. "Okay," he said, pulling out the card. "If I can only speak well of him once, what's the best thing I ever saw him do?" Lindsay said the soccer game. Caius said the card games, because Grandpa had let Caius win exactly once and never again, which Caius claimed was respectful. Henry turned each one over in his mind like a stone.

Then he remembered the apple tree. Two summers ago, the blossoms had come and gone and no fruit had followed, and everyone said the tree was dying. His grandfather had refused to cut it down. Instead he had set two of his hives beside it and explained that the bees needed to pollinate the blossoms before any apples could form, and that the windy spring had kept the wild bees away. The next year the tree had been so heavy with apples that a branch had cracked. Henry had thought it was luck at the time. Now he understood it had been his grandfather noticing an invisible problem and quietly fixing it.

"That's it," Henry said. "That's the one." The service began, and when Ms. Mansour caught his eye and nodded, he walked to the front with the card, though he barely looked at it. He told the apple tree story, including the cracked branch, and a ripple of soft laughter went through the chairs. He said the word eulogy once, explained in half a sentence what it meant, because his grandfather would have liked knowing that a fancy Greek word just meant speaking well of somebody, and that was a thing Grandpa had done for everyone, even a dying tree.

Afterward, Lindsay pressed something into his hand: a small synthetic flower, bright yellow, the kind that never fades. "For the tree story," she said. Henry carried it back to the fence and set it on the flat stone where the lichen grew, bright against all that gray. Caius clapped him on the shoulder. "You spoke well of him," Caius said. Henry looked out past the fence at the row of apple trees along the cemetery road, every one of them in bloom.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A result that shows the hypothesis was wrong is still a real scientific result and is worth reporting.
story:
Eli crouched beside the garden bed behind the garage, where eight bean plants stood in a stubborn row. Tomorrow morning the science fair boards had to be carried into the gym, and his board was still blank. His hypothesis, printed neatly at the top of his notebook, said that plants watered with sugar water would grow taller than plants watered with plain water, because the extra energy had to go somewhere. He had measured the sugar-fed plants every Sunday for three weeks. They were shorter. Every single one.

"What's that face?" Maxine asked, dropping onto the grass beside him with her clipboard. She was doing her project on which paper airplane design flew farthest, and her results had cooperated, which suddenly seemed unfair. "They look fine."

"They're losers," Eli said. "The sugar ones are four centimeters shorter. My hypothesis is wrong, and I don't have time to redo it." He poked the soil, which smelled damp and faintly of the molasses he had mixed into his watering can. Behind the fence, Mr. Romano was stacking flowerpots, and Eli asked him, half hoping for a miracle, whether he thought the plants might still catch up overnight.

"Plants don't sprint," Mr. Romano said, resting a pot on the fence rail. "That's a result, kid. A result that shows the hypothesis was wrong is still a real scientific result, and it's worth reporting." He picked up another pot and went back to his stacking, as if he had said nothing more remarkable than the weather.

Eli sat with that. He turned it over the way he turned over a rock in the creek, wondering what might be living underneath it. The fertilizer bag in the shed had bragged about containing a natural plant hormone that boosted growth, and he had read that sugar fed soil bacteria instead. Was that why the sugar plants looked pale and droopy while the plain-water plants stood buoyant and green, their leaves lifting in the evening breeze? He couldn't see the bacteria, but he could see the pattern: more sugar, shorter plants, every time. That was a rule hiding in his own data, and he had almost thrown it in the compost.

He ran inside and printed his board in bold letters: "What Happens When My Hypothesis Was Wrong." He drew a bar graph with the sugar plants low and the plain plants high, and a second panel on how he would budget his time next year to test two groups at once. Maxine leaned over the fence to look, holding a paper airplane.

"You're presenting the failure?" she said.

"I'm presenting the finding," Eli said, and taped the last chart to the board.

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Universal indicator changes to a range of different colours, and each colour matches a different pH number on a chart.
story:
Sawyer had twelve jars lined up on the kitchen table, and the litmus paper was telling him almost nothing.

"Red for acid, blue for base," Nia said, reading his notes upside down. "Which jar?"

"All of them, some of them, who knows." Sawyer held up a strip that had turned a polite shade of purple. The science fair was Thursday. Their project was supposed to be about the pH of household liquids, but litmus only gave two answers, and the judges wanted numbers. Rohan had already pointed this out twice, once in a text and once out loud, slowly, which felt like humiliation by instalment.

Mr. Kobayashi, who lived next door and taught chemistry at the high school, had dropped off a small bottle that morning. "Universal indicator," he'd said, and then he'd left for work without another word, which was either rude or efficient.

Sawyer uncapped it and added a few drops to the vinegar. The liquid went from clear to a red so definite it looked like an opinion. He tried the baking soda water next. It turned a deep blue-violet. Lemon juice went orange. The milk of magnesia, of all things, went a purple so dark it was nearly navy.

"So the colour is the answer," Nia said, frowning at the lineup. "But an answer to what?"

Sawyer found a folded chart tucked inside Mr. Kobayashi's bag, printed with a rainbow strip and numbers from zero to fourteen beside each colour. He matched red to the vinegar. "pH two," he said. He matched the navy magnesia. "About ten." The baking soda water read around nine. He could infer, then, that anything landing near orange or red was acidic, and anything drifting into the purples was a base, because the colours were marching along the numbers like a scale.

"Wait." Nina held up her phone. She was Nia. She was already photographing the jars. "So we get actual numbers for every single jar, and the litmus stuff goes where?"

"In the report as our first attempt," Sawyer said. "A sophisticated first attempt that ran into a wall."

Rohan arrived at four with his poster board under one arm. He looked at the rainbow lineup of jars, then at the chart, then at Sawyer. "You figured out the whole thing without me."

"You can cut the chart out and glue it to the poster."

"Deal." Rohan set down the board, then pointed at the last jar, a murky green one Sawyer hadn't labelled yet. "What's that one?"

Sawyer dropped in the indicator, watched the green hold steady, and slid the chart across the table. "You tell me."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: Demand for necessities, such as essential medicines, changes little when their price changes; economists call this inelastic demand.
story:
The line outside the arena already wrapped around the block when David arrived at six in the morning, and by seven it had doubled. Tatum stood three places ahead of him, hood up, hopping in place against the cold. "Forty dollars at the window," she said, "if we even get there." Behind them, a scalper in a gray jacket strolled past, holding up two fingers. "Two hundred each," he called softly, and David watched a man near the front peel off bills without even asking where the seats were.

By eight, the scalper was at four hundred. David kept doing the math in his head. The window price hadn't moved a cent, yet the price out here on the sidewalk kept climbing with every new person who joined the line, and every announcement from the loudspeaker that fewer seats remained. It was like watching a hidden rule work itself out in the open: the more people wanted what was running out, the more they'd pay. Tatum saw it too. "It's the opposite with the shirts," she said, pointing at a cart piled with last year's tour merchandise. "He started at twenty and now he's yelling ten. Nobody wants those. They're everywhere."

Across the street sat an all-night pharmacy, and David noticed a woman come out of it, clutching a white paper bag and staring at her receipt. She stood there a long moment, then walked back to the end of the ticket line, where a boy about David's age waited with an inhaler in his hand. She said something to him and ruffled his hair. Kyler, two spots behind David, followed David's gaze. "That's the third person from that pharmacy who looked sick about the price and bought the bag anyway," Kyler said. "The sign says the medicine went up again."

David watched a fourth customer do the same thing. He tried to fit it into his rule, the one that had explained the scalper and the shirt cart, and it wouldn't fit. Prices had risen, but the buying hadn't slowed at all, not even a little. With the shirts, a higher price had emptied the cart. With the medicine, a higher price changed nothing. He turned around. "Kyler, why do they keep buying it when it costs more?"

Kyler's older sister took economics, and Kyler shrugged. "She says medicine's different. People need it no matter what it costs. She calls that inelastic demand." That was all he said, but David turned the strange word over while the line shuffled forward.

The loudspeaker crackled: one hundred seats left. The scalper's price jumped to six hundred, and the shirt man yelled "Five dollars! Two for five!" At the pharmacy door, a fifth customer counted out cash for the same bag, the same price, without blinking. David reached the window just as it opened, slid his forty dollars through, and heard the printer hum. Tatum leaned over his shoulder as the tickets dropped into his hand. "Fifth row," she said, and pointed across the street at the pharmacy. "And that kid's mom is still in line to buy his medicine."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word Inuit means 'the people' in the Inuktitut language, and one person is called an Inuk.
story:
Louis had one job at Dakota's house: write the caption for their heritage wall project while Dakota and Jazmine argued about glue sticks. The wall was for the community centre, and their panel was about the North. Louis typed fast, because typing fast looked like working.

The photo showed a single man in a parka standing on sea ice, and Louis wrote underneath: "An Inuit hunter checks the ice." He sat back. Jazmine leaned over his shoulder, chewing a pretzel with great purpose.

"Wait," she said. "One guy. Isn't there a word for one?"

Louis had not considered this. He considered it now, staring at the photo as if the man might hold up a sign. "It's like moose," he tried. "One moose, ten moose, all moose."

"That's not a rule, that's a moose," said Dakota from the floor, where the glue stick negotiations had collapsed entirely.

Louis scrolled. He found an interview with the man in the photo, from a school website, three pages of him talking about his grandfather. Halfway down, the interviewer had made the same mistake, writing "an Inuit," and there was a correction in brackets. Louis read it twice, then a third time to be sure.

"Okay," he said. "So the word Inuit means 'the people,' in Inuktitut. And one person is an Inuk." He deleted his caption and started over. "This guy is an Inuk. His whole community, together, they're Inuit. If I call one person 'an Inuit,' I'm basically calling him a whole crowd of people by himself."

"Imagine the grocery bill," said Jazmine.

Dakota stood up and looked at the screen. "So our caption about the whole town uses Inuit, and the caption about one person uses Inuk."

"Exactly," said Louis. He typed it: "An Inuk hunter checks the ice while his community, the Inuit, wait for the season to turn." He read it aloud. It sounded, he thought, like something a person with real ambition would write, the kind of person who checked facts before pretending to be done.

Ms. Guo arrived at four to pick up her donated poster board, which had been consistent about being in her car all week and had finally made it into Dakota's kitchen. She read the caption over Louis's shoulder, and Louis held his breath, because Ms. Guo's face did not radiate approval so much as occasionally permit it.

"Hm," she said. "Who found the singular?"

"Me," said Louis. "By accident. Mostly."

"Good accidents are underrated," said Ms. Guo, and she carried her poster board out the door.

Jazmine picked up the glue stick and pointed it at Louis like a tiny ceremonial sword. "You realize this means you're the caption person forever now."

Louis looked at the wall, where twelve more photos waited with no words under them at all. "Then I demand a title," he said. "Chief of Captions. It's like moose. One chief, all chiefs."

"Just get typing," said Dakota.

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: Proportional representation more often produces coalition governments, because a single party rarely wins more than half the votes.
story:
The votes lay in three shoeboxes on the table at the community centre, one for each party in Ms. González's mock parliament. Alicia counted them twice, because the first time the numbers felt wrong. Purple Party, eleven votes. Orange Party, nine. Green Party, six. Twenty-six students had voted, and Ms. González had promised the afternoon would end with a government.

Anabel leaned over the boxes. "Purple wins. They got the most."

"That's first past the post," Alicia said. "Most votes takes everything. But we learned the other way today. Proportional representation. Purple should get about eleven seats out of twenty-six, Orange about nine, Green about six."

Ms. González had written the rules on the whiteboard, then sat in the corner with her tea and refused to say another word. "You figure it out," she had said. "Pretend I'm the Queen. I only sign things."

So Alicia handed out seats, folding paper strips and writing names on them. Anabel, who led Purple, grabbed her eleven strips and marched to the front table. "We're the government. Everyone else is opposition."

"Wait," said Hiba, from the Green Party. "Count your seats. You need thirteen to govern alone. You only have eleven."

Alicia checked the whiteboard. Half of twenty-six was thirteen. Nobody had thirteen. She ran her finger down the seat list again, slower this time, in case the numbers had shifted while she wasn't looking. They hadn't. The room went quiet except for the hum of the radiators.

"Then nobody's the government," Anabel said. "The Queen can't sign anything. We're stuck forever."

Alicia felt something click, the way a pattern does when you finally see it. "Not stuck. It happened the way the numbers said it would. When seats get shared out fairly, one party hardly ever gets more than half the votes, so the parties have to team up. Coalition. That's the word from the worksheet." She kept her voice steady, though her pulse was going fast. "Purple plus anyone gets past thirteen."

Anabel stared at her eleven strips, then at the Orange table. Orange stared back. The whole room waited.

"You'd want the library period extended," Anabel said at last. "We want the bake sale. Those aren't the same thing."

"They could both be in the budget," Hiba offered, slipping over with her six Green seats, agile in the way of someone who had been waiting all afternoon for exactly this moment. "Six seats is small, but it's enough to matter."

The three parties haggled over the paper strips, trading a library period for a bake sale, arguing about who would summarize the new laws for the Queen. When they finally carried their coalition agreement to the corner table, Ms. González read every line, stamped it, and said only, "About time."

Anabel held up the stamped page like a trophy. "Motion carried," she announced, "thirteen to twelve."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: In written dialogue, a new paragraph begins each time a different character starts speaking, so readers can tell who is talking.
story:
Carter slid his story across the table to Sean and waited. The writing club met in Mr. Jung's classroom after school on Thursdays, and today was the day they traded drafts. Carter's story was about two brothers in a rowboat caught in a turbulent storm, arguing about whether to row for shore or ride it out. He had worked on the argument scene for two full nights, and he was proud of it.

Sean read, frowning. Then he read it again. "Wait, who's talking here?" he asked, tapping the page. "The older brother says row for shore, and then something about the oars, and then something about the lightning, and it's all one big lump. I got lost. I thought the little brother said the lightning part, but then he'd be arguing with himself."

Carter leaned over and looked at his own paragraph. There it was, a solid block of speech with quotation marks stacked end to end, the two brothers trading lines without a break. No wonder Sean had evaporated right out of the story, gone like mist off the water. But how was a reader supposed to know who said what? Carter wondered if there was some trick to it, some pattern in real books.

He grabbed a library book from Mr. Jung's shelf, a novel he'd read twice, and flipped to a conversation. There. Every single time a new character opened their mouth, a new paragraph started. He flipped further. Same thing, page after page. "Look at this," Carter said, and Sean bent in. "A new paragraph begins each time a different character starts speaking."

"So that's how you can tell who's talking," Sean said slowly, running his finger down the page. "You don't even need names half the time."

Carter went back to his draft with a pencil. He broke the argument apart, gave each brother his own paragraph, and read it aloud in a low voice to test it. The words sounded like two people now. Sean listened, then grinned, because he'd been pushing all week to get his own story read aloud at the club showcase, and an argument scene this clear might earn him a spot.

Mr. Jung wandered past their table and skimmed the revised pages. He raised his eyebrows at Carter and said, "Much better. Read it to the group."

At the front of the room, Carter took a breath and began, "Row for shore," the older brother shouted.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During China's Qingming Festival, usually on April 4 or 5, families visit their ancestors' graves to clean them and leave offerings.
story:
Joseph had never swept a gravestone before, and he discovered it was harder than it looked. The brush kept skipping over the carved characters of his grandfather's name, so he slowed down and worked the bristles into each groove while his cousins, Kaius and Emmanuel, pulled weeds from the cracks around the base. Their whole family had driven two hours into the hills that morning, and now dozens of other families dotted the hillside too, all of them sweeping, wiping, and setting out food on the stones.

"Emmanuel says it's called Qingming," Kaius said, crouching beside Joseph with a fistful of grass. "Families visit their ancestors' graves, clean them, and leave offerings. It happens every year around April fourth or fifth." Emmanuel, who was thirteen like the rest of them but acted like he was thirty, nodded from behind the stone, where he was scrubbing off a smear of moss.

Joseph tested the bristles against the deepest groove one more time, then sat back on his heels. He had been thinking about something all morning, and this seemed like the moment to try it. Last spring, before Grandfather got sick, Joseph had chosen to stay home and finish a video game instead of going with him to the noodle shop where Grandfather had eaten every Saturday for thirty years. He had told himself there would be other Saturdays. Now he wanted to know if he could still send something, even one way.

"Grandfather always ordered extra chili oil," Joseph said. "The waiter would warn him every single time, and every single time he'd say, 'I know, that's why I ordered it.'" He pulled from his backpack the small jar he had taken from Grandfather's kitchen cupboard, with his mother's permission, plus a stack of paper bowls he had bought at the corner store after school. His idea was simple: if the families on this hill were leaving offerings of food, then maybe a bowl of noodles with chili oil, mixed the way Grandfather liked it, could go on the stone too.

He assembled it right there. The steam fluctuated in the breeze, curling and straightening, curling and straightening, as if the wind couldn't make up its mind. Emmanuel watched with the expression of a scientist observing a radical new experiment, and Kaius said, "That's the first time I've ever been jealous of a gravestone."

Their grandmother came over, and Joseph held his breath. She looked at the bowl, then at the jar, and something in her face shifted. She said, "He'd complain it needed more chili," and knelt down and added another spoonful herself.

By the time they packed up, the afternoon sun had made nearly a full revolution around the hilltop, lighting the far side of the valley. Whether the noodles reached anyone, Joseph couldn't know, and he decided he didn't need to. He picked up the empty jar to bring home, and Kaius asked, "Same time next April?"

"Same time," Joseph said. "But I'm bringing two jars."

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: A sharp knife is safer than a dull one because it needs less pressure to cut, so it is less likely to slip off the food.
story:
Victor stood at the stainless steel counter in Ms. Virtanen's cooking class, staring down an onion like it owed him money. Chopping was mandatory this unit, and the sauce they were making had to be from scratch, no jars, no shortcuts. He curled his fingers into the claw grip the way the diagram on the wall showed, knuckles forward like a boxer's fists, and pressed the knife down. The blade squashed the onion half instead of slicing it. He leaned harder, and the knife slid sideways with a squeak and nearly skated off the cutting board.

Spencer, one station over, watched the whole thing. "You're going to lose a thumb," he said, dicing his own onion in quick, easy strokes.

"My knife is broken," Victor said, holding it up. The edge looked fine, but something about it felt wrong, like a spoon wearing a knife costume.

Ms. Virtanen passed by, glanced at his mangled onion, and swapped his blade for a different one from the rack without a word. Victor set the new knife on the onion, barely pushed, and it sank clean through. A perfect little dice fell away. He blinked. Same hand, same claw grip, completely different result. What had changed? He looked at the two knives, turning them over, wondering if his eyes were missing something they should be able to see.

It reminded him of last summer, when he'd tried to cut a tomato at home with the old knife from the back of the drawer. He'd pushed and pushed, and the blade had skidded right off the slippery skin and jabbed the counter. His dad had handed him the sharp one, and the tomato had opened like it wanted to. Victor had thought at the time that he'd just been clumsy. Now he wondered if the knife itself had been the problem all along. He tested it: with the sharp knife he used almost no pressure, and nothing slipped. With his old one, he'd had to shove, and the shoving was what sent it sliding. A sharp knife is safer, he realized, because it needs less pressure, so it's less likely to slip off the food.

"Dude," Victor said to Spencer, waving the sharp knife like evidence at a trial. "A sharp one is actually the safe one. It doesn't slip because you don't have to push."

"Congratulations," Spencer said. "Now prioritize the sauce before we run out of class time."

The onion hit the hot oil with a hiss, and Victor leaned in to watch it turn glassy and gold.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Going from 40 percent to 50 percent is a rise of 10 percentage points but a 25 percent increase, so the two phrases describe the same change.
story:
Jackson taped the two news stories side by side on Ms. Oliveira's classroom door and waited for her with his arms folded. The bell hadn't rung yet, and the hallway smelled like wet snow from everyone's boots.

"Two papers, one poll," he said when she arrived. "This one says the team's free throws went from 40 percent to 50 percent, a rise of 10 points. This one says the same thing, same numbers, but it calls it a 25 percent increase. Ten and twenty-five. Somebody's lying."

Ms. Oliveira read both clippings, then handed them back. "That's a real puzzle, Jackson. But I don't think either reporter made it up. You're welcome to figure it out."

He tried the obvious explanation first: maybe the poll was different, or one paper made a rounding error. He checked the dates, the team name, and every number he could find. Both stories matched exactly. If neither story was wrong, he thought, then both numbers had to be true at once, which felt impossible, like two answers orbiting the same question.

At lunch he dragged his clippings to the corner table where Christine was stacking her tray. "Read these. Tell me I'm not crazy."

She read them twice. "They're both saying the same thing."

"But ten isn't twenty-five," Jackson said. He grabbed a napkin and wrote it out. "Forty to fifty." Christine frowned at the napkin like it might be hiding something.

That afternoon in the gym, the coach had them shoot twenty free throws each, and Jackson counted his makes on his fingers like money. When he missed his last five, Allison laughed from the foul line. "You're plague-level bad today."

"Say that again," Jackson said slowly, an idea turning over in his mind. He walked to the bench and did the arithmetic twice, then a third time, because the first two times it seemed too strange to trust. Then he ran back across the gym floor.

"Ten points and twenty-five percent," he told Christine after practice, holding up his wrinkled napkin. "Same change. Forty to fifty. Two ways of saying it. It sounds like a lie, but it's true." He smoothed the napkin on the bleachers between them.

Christine looked at it, then at him. "So both reporters were right?"

"Both right," Jackson said, and folded the napkin into his pocket like a ticket he'd won.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Many museums ask visitors not to touch objects, because oils and salts from skin build up over time and can stain or damage the surfaces.
story:
The fire station smelled like rubber boots and old coffee, and Penelope had exactly forty minutes before the bus left, because Mr. Gill had promised the driver they would be gone by noon. Mr. Gill's worksheet was due on the bus, all five questions filled in, and question four was the one she could not answer: "What does this station preserve from its past, and how?" The tour had rushed past the modern trucks and stopped in the back room, where the guide had waved at a scarred wooden desk and a brass pole before hurrying off to answer someone's question about dalmatians.

Hayden reached out to run his hand along the desk's edge, the way you test a railing. "Don't," Nevaeh said, grabbing his sleeve. "Museums ask people not to touch stuff like this. Oils and salts from your skin build up over time and can stain or damage the surfaces." Hayden pulled his hand back and wiped it on his jeans as if his fingers had already done something wrong. "It's just a desk," he muttered, but he kept his hands in his pockets after that.

Penelope looked at the desk more closely. One end of it was pale and dry, the way old untreated wood looks, but the other end, the end nearest the brass pole, had a dark, shiny patch the shape of a handprint, almost like it had been soaked. She thought about that. If oils and salts from skin built up over time, then the dark patch could be decades of firefighters grabbing that same corner while sliding down the pole, each hand leaving a little behind. It was like a pattern you could read backwards: the stain was the effect, and the hands were the hidden cause.

She decided to test it. The desk was off limits now that she knew the rule, but her own sunglasses in her pocket had a smudge she'd been wiping with her thumb all week. She breathed on the lens and looked at the light: a cloudy print exactly where her thumb always landed, faint but there, building. She had never once seen the oils leave her skin, yet there was proof on the glass. "Okay," she whispered, and Hayden asked what she was doing with her sunglasses in a dark fire station. "Proving something," she said.

She wrote her answer for question four: the station preserves the old desk and pole by keeping hands off them, because skin oils and salts build up over time and stain the surfaces, which is why the shiny patch near the pole looks the way it does. When Mr. Gill collected the worksheets on the bus, he read hers twice. "I've taken three classes here," he said, "and nobody ever noticed the handprint before." Nevaeh leaned over the seat. "Show me," she said, and Penelope turned around as the bus pulled out, pointing back toward the station doors.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In 1972 James Woodward proposed writing 'Deaf' with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase 'deaf' for the hearing condition itself.
story:
Andrew spread the poster paper across Colton's kitchen table and weighted the corners with mugs from the cupboard. The sign-language club needed a banner for its booth at the school fair, and Colton had volunteered him because, as he put it, "You have neat handwriting and no other plans on a Saturday."

The design was easy: two hands, blue and gold, and the words JOIN THE SIGN LANGUAGE CLUB in big letters across the top. Andrew had gotten that far when Colton tapped the paper and pointed at the smaller line underneath, the one that read "Open to deaf students and everyone else." Colton wrote something in his notebook and turned it around: Should that d be capital?

Andrew stared at the word. Lowercase seemed right for an adjective, the way you'd write "tall students" or "new students." But Colton's question had a look behind it, like there was a trapdoor under the word and Colton knew exactly where it was. "Does it matter?" Andrew asked, and Colton grinned in a way that meant it absolutely mattered.

They raided Colton's bookshelf, which was stacked with books about sign language and Deaf history, and Andrew found a chapter that mentioned James Woodward. In 1972, Woodward had proposed writing Deaf with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase deaf for the hearing condition itself. Andrew read it twice. So the little d described ears, and the big D described people who belonged to something, a whole culture built around a language, with its own schools and jokes and stories that Colton's family told at dinner with everyone laughing in signs.

Andrew tested his idea out loud. "So if the poster says the club is open to anyone, lowercase deaf covers the condition, but anyone who feels part of the culture can claim the big D." Colton thought about it, then nodded slowly, then shook his head and wrote: Make it capital. The club is about the culture, not about ears. Andrew got it. He had been thinking of deaf as a fact about a person's body, when Colton's club was really about a people.

Mr. Demir, the club's advisor, stopped by to drop off markers, and Andrew showed him the finished banner. "JOIN THE SIGN LANGUAGE CLUB," it read, "everyone welcome, Deaf and hearing." Mr. Demir, who never prescribed rules he could let students discover for themselves, only raised an eyebrow at the capital D and asked, "Whose motivation was that, capitalizing it?" Andrew pointed at Colton, and Colton pointed back at him. "Both of us," Andrew said. Mr. Demir smiled and said the change might be gradual for some people, but the poster looked ready to change a few minds in one afternoon. Andrew rolled up the banner, tucked it under his arm, and carried it out the door.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: 20/40 vision means you must stand 20 feet away to read letters that a person with normal eyesight can read from 40 feet.
story:
The waiting room of the eyeglasses store had a chart on the wall with rows of letters that shrank as they went down, and Sofia sat across from it while the optician flipped lenses in a frame that clamped onto her head like a bug. Her friend Lucille had sent her a text that morning: "Good luck. Also, did you finish the science homework? I only wrote two sentences about the extinction of the dinosaurs and Mr. Nwosu will notice." Sofia had typed back that she had written a whole paragraph and left out the part where she had copied half of it.

"Read the smallest line you can," the optician said.

"F, P, T, O, and then it gets fuzzy," Sofia said.

"Right eye, that's 20/40," the woman said, and wrote it on a card.

Sofia stared at the numbers. Lucille had told her once that her own vision was 20/20, and Sofia had assumed bigger numbers were better, the way a score of 40 beats a score of 20. Now she was not so sure, because nobody in the store looked impressed. She decided to test it. The chart hung on the wall and there were floor tiles, so she counted tiles to what she guessed was about 20 feet and stood there. At that distance the F and the P were clear, but when she walked forward to half that distance, they were just as clear and the next line down started to come into focus too. The letter she had been unable to read from across the room was easy up close. So the second number had something to do with how far away the letters were.

She walked back to the chair and asked the optician, "Does 20/40 mean I have to stand 20 feet away to read letters that a person with normal eyesight can read from 40 feet?"

"That's exactly what it means," the woman said.

So the bigger number was worse, not better. Sofia paraphrased it in her head to make sure she had it: normal eyes read the line at double her distance, which meant her eyes were weaker, not stronger. She felt her ears go warm, because she had told Lucille last week that her eyes were probably better than everyone's. She pulled out her phone and texted: "Correction. 20/40 is not a good score. My eyes are the opposite of good. Also I will help you with the dinosaur thing."

The frame choices were on a spinning rack near the window. Sofia tried on a pair of black rectangles, then a pair of round wire ones that made her look like a substitute teacher. In the mirror, the price tags hung down over her cheeks, and each pair gave her a distinct reflection of the same face, one slightly squashed, one slightly wide. She picked the black rectangles because they stayed put when she shook her head.

The glasses would be ready in an hour, so she and her mother walked to the sandwich place next door. Through the window Sofia noticed that the sign across the street had words on it, actual words, not a gray smear with colored edges. She had been reading that street for years without knowing it was saying anything.

When she picked up the glasses and stepped outside, she stopped on the sidewalk and read the sign out loud. "Lucille," she said to her mother, pointing, "there's a Lucille in that sign. Lucille's Bakery. It's been there the whole time."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of children's bones, are weaker than the bone around them, which is why young athletes have limits on repetitive stress.
story:
The score was tied in the fifth inning when Aubrey spotted Coach holding up three fingers toward the dugout, and she knew exactly what that meant. Kyan, their best pitcher, had only three pitches left. She bounced on the bench, cleats scraping the dirt, because if Kyan could hold the Pirates scoreless here at Riverside Park, the Rockets would take first place for the first time all season.

Kyan threw two fastballs and got two outs, then walked a batter on his last pitch. When he jogged to the bench, Coach met him with a hand on his shoulder. "That's your limit for today, and for the week. Sit down."

Kyan yanked off his cap. "I feel fine! My arm's not even sore." Aubrey watched Coach shake his head and walk away, and something about it bothered her. Kyan had only thrown, what, sixty pitches? She pulled out the scorebook and counted the tallies. Sixty-one. Last week he'd thrown fifty-eight, and the week before that, fifty-five. There was a pattern, and she wanted to know the rule behind it.

She remembered the fourth game of the season, back in April, when the Rockets had been getting crushed and Coach had refused to send Kyan back out for a second inning of relief. Leonardo had joked that a swarm of bees had somehow thwarted the plan, but Aubrey had noticed that Mr. Pérez, their neighbor, was at that game too, and he'd nodded like Coach had done the right thing. Mr. Pérez knew everything about baseball. He'd grown up playing near the old settlement fields on the other side of the creek, and he refereed adult leagues on weekends.

After the game, which the Rockets won 4-3 on a wild pitch, Aubrey found Mr. Pérez stacking coolers by the settlement trail. "Why does Kyan have a pitch count?" she asked. "He's not tired."

Mr. Pérez laughed. "It's not about being tired. Kids his age still have growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of the bones, and that cartilage is weaker than the bone around it. That's why young athletes have limits on repetitive stress. Throw too much, and the weakest part gives out."

"So the rule isn't about the arm being sore at all," Aubrey said slowly. "It's about a part nobody can see."

"That's it exactly," Mr. Pérez said.

On Saturday, Aubrey tested the idea. She brought the scorebook to practice and asked Kyan to help her chart every pitcher on the team, not just the totals but the days between outings. Leonardo joined in, waving an aerosol can of sunscreen over the charts and reading the label out loud. "Caution, flammable, keep away from open flame," he announced. "Which means don't set these on fire, in case anyone was planning to." He set it down and drew a smiley face next to Kyan's name.

By the end of practice the chart showed something real: the two players who pitched two games in a row had been rested for four days after, every time, without anyone saying why out loud. Coach saw the chart draped over the fence, and he tapped the paper with one finger.

"You figured out my rotation," he said.

"Growth plates," Aubrey said.

He grinned and pulled a whistle from his pocket. "Then you're my new scorekeeper. First job: tell Leonardo the sunflower seeds by the concession stand are for eating, not for juggling."

Leonardo caught the bag one-handed and held it up like a trophy. "Too late. Already juggling."

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: When a dependent person stops using nicotine, withdrawal can bring irritability, anxiety, trouble concentrating and strong cravings.
story:
Harrison locked the bathroom door, set his cue cards on the edge of the sink, and faced the mirror.
