"When nicotine gets into the brain," he told his reflection, "it hijacks the reward pathway, the system that normally responds to food and other good things." His voice cracked on "pathway," so he tried again, slower. Ms. Tremblay had picked him to explain it to the class on Friday, and he was his own tutor until then, drilling in the one room where nobody would interrupt.

Except somebody was interrupting the whole house. His dad had quit smoking on Monday, and by Wednesday he was snapping at everything. That morning he had grumbled at the toaster, lost his keys twice, and snapped at Harrison's little sister for humming. He couldn't seem to focus on the grocery list. Harrison kept wondering: was that just a bad week, or was it connected to the quitting? He had a suspicion, but a suspicion wasn't proof. He needed to test it.

He spread his cue cards on the bathroom floor and made a list on the back of the "Withdrawal" card: grumpy, jumpy, forgetful, dying for a cigarette. Then he copied the same words onto a second card and carried it downstairs at dinner. He watched, not staring, just noticing. Dad fidgeted with his fork, forgot he'd already passed the peas, and got short with Mom about nothing. Every item, checked off, one by one. Harrison chewed a mouthful of rice slowly, letting it all digest while he watched.

He called Sidney after dinner. "You know how my dad's been grumpy all week? I think it's withdrawal. When a dependent person stops using nicotine, they can get irritability, anxiety, trouble concentrating, and strong cravings." "Wait," Sidney said, "you mean he's not just in a mood?" "That's what I thought at first," Harrison said. "But it matches, all four things, and it started the day he quit." Archie, on three-way, chimed in. "So it's kind of voluntary, him quitting, but then the withdrawal isn't something he chooses?" "Exactly," Harrison said, surprised Archie had gotten there first.

On Friday, Harrison stood at the front of the class and explained the reward pathway, how nicotine trains the brain to demand more. Then he added, "And here's the part nobody tells you. My dad quit five days ago, and he's had irritability, anxiety, trouble concentrating, and serious cravings all week. So if someone you know gets grumpy after quitting, it might not be about you." Ms. Tremblay raised her eyebrows and wrote something on her clipboard.

That afternoon, Harrison found his dad pacing the kitchen with unopened gum in his fist. "Ms. Tremblay says it gets easier after the first couple of weeks," Harrison said carefully. Dad looked at him for a long moment, then laughed, a real laugh, the first one all week. "You did a report on me?" "Sort of," Harrison said, and slid the gum across the counter toward him.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In one-point perspective, lines that face you squarely, like window tops and doorframes on a building's front, stay perfectly horizontal or vertical.
story:
Jaxson slid his ruler across the paper and drew another line toward the dot in the middle of the page. That dot was the vanishing point, and every sidewalk edge, every roofline that ran away from him, had to aim straight at it. Ms. Bekele had promised that by the end of class everyone would have a street that looked like it went somewhere, and Jaxson wanted his to go somewhere amazing.

"I finished!" Alexa announced two desks over, holding up her drawing like a trophy. Then her face fell. "Wait. Why do my buildings look like they're falling over?"

Jaxson leaned over. Her street had shops, awnings, a mailbox, all slanting toward the dot. Every single line was tilted, even the fronts of the buildings that faced her squarely. The window tops pointed downhill. The doorframes leaned sideways. The whole block looked like it was sliding off the page.

He stared at it, and something clicked open in his memory. Last summer, before the perspective unit, he had tried to draw his grandmother's house from across the street. He'd slanted the porch roof, slanted the window frames, everything, and the house had come out wobbly too. He'd thrown that drawing away thinking he just had bad hands. Now he formulated a quick idea to test: maybe the fronts of buildings, the parts facing you directly, were different from the parts running away from you. He grabbed a scrap paper and drew a simple box front-on. The edges going back in depth slanted toward a dot. The edges across the front of the box? He kept those perfectly horizontal and vertical. The box sat solid on the page. He drew another, then a whole row, and none of them fell over.

"Try this," he said, spinning the scrap toward Alexa. "The lines on the front of the shop, the window tops and doorframes, keep them horizontal or vertical. Only the lines running away from you go to the dot."

Alexa erased her tilting fronts, redrew them straight across and straight up and down, and gasped. "It's a real street! Jaxson, it's a real street!"

"Trade secrets," Hendrik said gravely from the next row, "will cost you a seat at lunch."

"You can have two seats," Alexa said, already darkening her doorframe with a fresh ruler line, "if you tell nobody my first draft ever existed."

"First drafts like that are basically extinct," Jaxson said, "the moment the good one appears." He went back to his own street and drew his storefronts front-on, ruled them straight, and added a bicycle leaning against a doorframe that stood, at last, exactly upright.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses, so they do not help cure a cold or the flu.
story:
Lincoln sat at the kitchen table wrapped in his grandmother's quilt, staring at the same glass of orange juice he had ignored for an hour. His throat felt like sandpaper, his nose was a faucet, and worst of all, tomorrow was the regional chess tournament, the one he had earned a spot in by beating Nikola twice in the qualifiers. His mom set a bowl of soup in front of him and felt his forehead with the back of her hand.

"Maybe Dr. Patel can call in antibiotics," Lincoln said, spooning steam toward his face. "Nikola got antibiotics last year when he was sick, and he was back at school in two days. If I got some today, I could still play tomorrow."

His mom tilted her head. "You want me to call and ask?"

"Please." He sneezed into a tissue, then added, "It's the tournament. Coach says it's a privilege to be seeded this high, and I don't want to waste it."

While his mom made the call in the hallway, Lincoln heard a knock. Nikola stood at the door holding a thermos and a paper bag, and behind him was Trystan, balancing a chessboard under one arm. They came in and crowded the kitchen, Nikola pouring hot lemon tea that smelled sharp and sweet.

"Nikola," Lincoln said, "when you took antibiotics, what did you actually have?"

"A strep throat," Nikola said. "Mr. Shin explained it to the whole science class afterward, actually. But wait, I thought you missed that day."

Lincoln's brain, foggy as it was, lurched into gear. Strep. He pulled his laptop across the table and typed, sniffling. Trystan leaned over his shoulder. The screen filled with the answer, and Lincoln read it out loud, his voice cracking. "Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses, so they don't help cure a cold or the flu." He sat back. "Strep is bacteria. That's why Nikola got better fast. But this," he pointed at his own red nose, "is a virus. Antibiotics would do nothing. I could take the whole bottle and I'd still be sneezing through the tournament."

His mom came back in, phone in hand. "Dr. Patel said the same thing, honey. Rest and fluids."

Lincoln pushed the soup closer and took a spoonful. It burned pleasantly going down. He tested one small idea out loud, ticking it off. "So if it's a virus, my immune system does the work, and sleeping is basically my move. If I sleep all afternoon and all tonight, maybe I'm functional by nine a.m."

"Functional enough to lose to me in round two," Trystan said, setting up the board. "I registered as an alternate."

"You're infectious, you know," Nikola said, backing up a step and grinning.

Lincoln laughed, which turned into a cough, which turned into Nikola patting his back and sliding the tea closer. "Okay, board away, germ boy. We'll set up a video call tomorrow so you can watch us play."

"Round two," Trystan said, snapping a pawn onto the table, "is mine."

"We'll see," Lincoln croaked, and raised his spoon like a sword.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: Going to bed and waking up at about the same time every day, including weekends, helps keep the body's internal clock, called the circadian rhythm, steady.
story:
Peyton loved Saturdays at Grandma's house, mostly because nobody woke her up. She slept until noon, ate cold pizza on the porch, and texted Giselle about nothing in particular. But on Monday mornings back home, her body felt like a phone at two percent battery. Her stomach knotted up before she even got on the bus, and last week she'd nearly cried over a missing math worksheet. She couldn't see what was causing it, which was the part that bugged her most.

"I think you just hate Mondays," Giselle said when Peyton described it at lunch. "Everyone does. It's basically a law."

Peyton didn't dismiss the idea out loud, but she didn't buy it either. Jasleen was fine on Mondays, and Peyton hadn't hated Mondays back in September, when soccer practice had forced her to bed early every night. Something had changed since then. She started keeping a note in her phone: bedtime, wake time, and how her stomach felt before school. By Thursday she had a suspicion, but she needed more data.

That weekend she was back at Grandma's, who was sorting seed catalogs at the kitchen table. "Still planning your vegetable garden?" Peyton asked, picking up a catalog with a cover full of tomato photographs. Grandma nodded and said agriculture had been her whole childhood, waking before dawn to help on the farm, every day, no exceptions. "Even Sundays?" Peyton asked. Grandma laughed. "Especially Sundays. The cows didn't know what a weekend was."

That night Peyton lay in the guest room bed scrolling on her phone, and her stomach was already doing its tight little Monday rehearsal, even though Monday was two days away. She mentioned it to Jasleen on a video call, and Jasleen read something off a health website: keeping the same sleep and wake times every day, weekends included, kept the body steady. "It's called your circadian rhythm," Jasleen said, pronouncing it carefully. Peyton sat straight up. Same time every day. Like the cows. Like soccer season, when she'd gone to bed at ten and gotten up at seven, even after Saturday games, because her dad drove her to early practice. The knot in her stomach had never shown up back then.

So she ran a test on herself. Friday night at Grandma's, she set an alarm for 7:30, turned her phone face down at ten, and did the slow breathing thing Ms. Quinn had shown the whole class after the fire drill: in for four counts, out for six. When the tight feeling crept in, she breathed through it instead of scrolling past it. Saturday morning she woke up tired but not wrecked. Sunday she did it again, even though Grandma offered pancakes at nine and Peyton had already been awake for ninety minutes.

Monday morning, on the bus, Peyton filled in her phone note: stomach, calm; brain, awake. It might be temporary, she knew, one good day out of many bad ones. But she'd already decided. Next Saturday at Grandma's, the alarm was staying on.

"Seven-thirty again?" Giselle texted her that afternoon.

Peyton typed back, "Same time every day. Even weekends."

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: No number of white swans can prove that all swans are white, but seeing a single black swan proves that claim false.
story:
Brody set his toast crust on the counter on purpose, the way he had every morning that week, and then walked to the doorway and counted to sixty. When he came back, the crust was gone. He had done this four times now, and every time the crust disappeared.

His hypothesis, which he had written on a napkin and taped inside the cupboard door, was that the dog ate it. The problem was that he could not actually see the dog do it. The dog, a small brown mutt named Patches, was shut in the laundry room every morning until Brody's mother left for work, and the crust vanished anyway. So the dog was out. That was the only thing he knew for sure.

He texted his friend Xavier about it after school.

Xavier wrote back: "this is like the swan thing mr joshi put on the board. No number of white swans can prove that all swans are white, but seeing a single black swan proves that claim false."

Brody read the message twice, then typed: "so if i watch the crust a hundred times and don't see who takes it, that proves nothing. but if i catch the thief once, i know for sure it wasn't the dog."

"exactly," Xavier wrote. "also you should get a sophisticated trap. flour everywhere. my brother did that for the cookie thief. it was me. i have the face of a criminal on camera."

Brody skipped the flour. Instead, the next morning he set out the crust and stood very still at the far end of the kitchen, next to the fridge, where the counter met the wall in a shadow. He held his phone up like he was checking the time. He waited. Four minutes. Five.

The cupboard under the sink, the one with the gap where the pipe went through the wall, made a small scratching sound. Then a gray mouse came out, walked along the baseboard, stood up on its hind legs at the corner of the counter, and dragged the crust down off the edge. It disappeared behind the toaster with the whole thing.

Brody lowered the phone. He crossed "dog" off the napkin and wrote "mouse" above it. Then he thought about Xavier's message again. He went back and added, at the bottom, "one crust still there would prove dog wrong. one mouse proves dog wrong. a hundred missing crusts prove nothing."

At dinner he told his mother the verdict, and she said they would get traps. Patches, let out of the laundry room, came over and put his chin on Brody's knee.

"Sorry, buddy," Brody said. "Not you this time." He slipped him a piece of crust anyway.

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Blue litmus paper turns red when dipped in an acid, and red litmus paper turns blue when dipped in a base.
story:
Piper laid her supplies across the kitchen table: a roll of paper towels, a box of baking soda, a bottle of vinegar, a carton of milk, and two small stacks of paper strips she had cut herself, red and blue. Ms. Gagnon had assigned the whole class a pH project for the science fair, and Piper had volunteered to build the booth because she wanted the blue ribbon more than she had wanted anything all year.

Then she found the note tucked inside the box of baking soda. It was from her friend Izabella, who had taken the supplies home the night before to help cut the strips. "Piper," it read, "my little brother got into the kitchen while I was working. I think he mixed up the strips. Some of the red ones and blue ones might have switched stacks. Sorry! Also my family is helping our new neighbours, who are refugees from Syria, so I might be late tomorrow." Piper stared at the two stacks. If the strips were mixed up, her whole demonstration would be wrong in front of everyone.

She sat down and thought. She could not see any difference between the strips just by looking, but there had to be a way to find out what each one was. Then she remembered the one thing she knew for certain: everyone in the class had been unanimous about vinegar during practice. It was an acid. If she dipped a strip in vinegar and it turned red, that strip was the blue kind, because that was the test: blue litmus paper turns red when dipped in an acid, and red litmus paper turns blue when dipped in a base.

She grabbed a strip from the "blue" stack and dunked it in a saucer of vinegar. Nothing happened. It stayed red. So that strip was actually a red one, mixed into the wrong pile. She tested another, and it turned red the moment it touched the liquid, which meant it was truly blue. Strip by strip, she sorted them, dipping and checking, building two honest stacks. Then she tried baking soda mixed with water, and a true red strip turned blue right before her eyes.

When Izabella arrived the next morning, Piper emphasized the pile of tested strips with both hands. "Every single one is sorted," she said. "Your brother actually helped. I understand the whole thing now, and I couldn't say that yesterday." Izabella laughed and hugged her.

At the science fair, a judge stopped at Piper's booth and dipped the blue strip into the vinegar herself. It turned red, clean and bright as a tiny flag.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Some element symbols come from Latin names, such as Fe for iron, from the Latin word ferrum.
story:
Julia slid the giant paper periodic table across the lab table and pinned the corner with her elbow before it could curl up again. Mr. Bui had promised that anyone who could correctly find the number of protons in five elements of his choosing would get to run the demo at the front of the room on Friday, and Julia wanted that more than she had wanted anything that week. The rule seemed simple: the atomic number up top of each box told you the protons. Sodium, eleven. Oxygen, eight. She felt almost smug.

Then Mr. Bui's scavenger hunt sheet said "iron," and Julia's whole plan fell apart. She ran her finger down the columns looking for an I. There was iodine, already claiming the symbol I, and there was iridium, smugly wearing Ir, but no iron anywhere. Ember leaned over from the next table, holding her own sheet. "I'm stuck on iron too," she said. "And if I don't finish this, I can't be your partner for the demo, and I already told my little brother I'd bring home the vinegar-and-baking-soda volcano trick." That was Ember's want, and Julia took it as seriously as her own. "Then we collaborate," Julia said. "You take the left side of the table, I take the right, and we look for anything that could mean iron."

Ananya, organizing the beakers at the supply shelf, called over without turning around. "Are you two hunting for iron? Because I found something last night that will make you feel like a peasant who just discovered electricity." She walked over waving a folded note she had written to herself in the margin of her notebook, and Julia read it aloud: "Dear future Ananya, iron is Fe. Not I. It comes from the Latin word ferrum. Signed, present Ananya, who was also confused." Julia laughed and went back to the table.

She found the box labeled Fe, and there it was, atomic number 26. Twenty-six protons, hidden inside every atom of a metal she could see in the door hinge, the chair legs, the fence outside. She tested her idea on another row to make sure the pattern held: gold, Au, also Latin, 79. Silver, Ag, 47. Copper, Cu, 29. Each symbol sat in its box like a nickname with a story behind it, and the number above it kept its promise every time.

By Friday Julia and Ember stood at the front table, filling a bottle while the class counted down. "Twenty-six protons," Ember announced, holding up the steel wool, "in every single strand of this." Julia struck the match, and the wool bloomed into a small, bright, coherent glow that made the whole second row lean forward in their seats.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Many of the world's hot deserts lie near 30 degrees north or south of the equator, where sinking air warms up and dries out.
story:
The trail climbed through pines until Ms. Whitehead called a rest stop at a granite outcrop, and Layla dropped her pack with a thud. Inside it, rolled tight, were two graphs she'd printed at the library: one for the Sahara, one for the Amazon. Her project was due Monday, and she still couldn't answer the question Ms. Whitehead had written at the top of the assignment sheet. Compare the climates. Explain what makes them different, and why.

The graphs themselves were easy. The desert's rainfall bars were stubs, barely visible except one slightly taller bar in a single month. The rainforest's bars climbed like a wall. The temperature lines told the other half: the desert line zigzagged between scorching days and cold nights, while the rainforest line ran flat and warm, month after month. Layla knew all that. What she didn't know was why. Rainforests huddled near the equator, sure. But deserts weren't at the equator, and they weren't scattered randomly either. She'd noticed something on the classroom globe last week, and she kept turning it over in her mind.

She had stayed late on Tuesday, spinning the globe slowly with one finger while the janitor worked down the hall. The Sahara. Then, below the equator, the Kalahari and the Australian deserts. Then Arabia, and the Atacama on the west coast of South America. She'd grabbed a sticky note and marked them, then stood back. The marks made two belts, one north of the equator and one south, and both belts sat at about the same distance from the middle of the globe. She'd folded the sticky note into her pocket without telling anyone, in case she was wrong.

"Earth to Layla," Conor said, sitting down beside her. He had his binoculars around his neck, the way he'd had them all morning, because he wanted a photo of a pileated woodpecker before lunch. He'd been planning this hike for two weeks and had told her twice that it was not a trivial goal, it was the whole point of walking six kilometres. "You're staring at paper like it owes you money."

"Look at this globe app," she said, pulling out her phone. She opened the map and traced the big deserts with her fingertip. "Tell me what you see."

Conor squinted. "Sand. Lots of sand."

"No, look at where they are. All of them." She waited, letting him find it the way she had, and for a moment nobody spoke. Somewhere downslope, water dripped off a ledge, steady as rain.

"They line up," Conor said slowly. "In two bands."

Layla checked the map's latitude scale with her thumb, the way she'd checked the globe. "About thirty degrees north, and thirty degrees south. That's where they sit." She thought of the graph in her pack, the stubby rainfall bars. It fit, and fitting it made the back of her neck prickle. "Ms. Whitehead said one thing I wrote down. Where air sinks in those belts, it warms up and dries out. So the rain never comes." She said it out loud for the first time, testing it, and it held.

Ms. Whitehead, who had been inspecting the trail register by the old lodge, called back to them that the park service planned to renovate the building next summer, and then asked what they were studying so intently. "Whether that dry-belt thing is a real phenomenon or a coincidence," Layla said. "I'm going to test it tonight. I'll pick three deserts I didn't mark before and check their latitudes on the map."

"If they're all near thirty," Conor said, standing up, binoculars rising, "you've got your answer."

Behind him, a red-crested bird hammered at a dead pine, and Conor spun toward it so fast he nearly fell off the outcrop.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: On a care label, an empty triangle means any bleach may be used, while a triangle with a cross through it means the garment must not be bleached.
story:
Gabriel stood in front of the washing machine with his mother's laundry basket and a feeling that this should be simpler than it looked. His mom had left for a work trip, and he had promised to handle his own clothes for the week. The basket held a tangle of jeans, socks, towels and one striped shirt that had gone grey in a way he hated.

He dumped everything on the laundry room floor and began making piles, darks in one heap, whites and lights in another, towels in a third, because towels shed fuzz onto everything and he was tired of fuzzy shirts. Sydney, who lived two houses down, had wandered over and sat on the dryer eating an apple. "You're doing it wrong," Sydney said, which was not helpful.

"Then show me right," Gabriel said. Sydney only shrugged and kept chewing.

The problem was the striped shirt. It was mostly white, so it belonged with the lights, but the stripes had faded and the whole thing looked dingy. Gabriel remembered the jug of bleach under the sink, the one his mom used on the white towels. He reached for it, then paused. Last summer a red sock had turned the whole load pink, and that disaster had been only temporary compared to what bleach might do. He turned the shirt inside out and hunted along the seam until he found the care label.

There were little symbols on it. A tub of water, a square with a circle, and two triangles. On his grey sweatpants the label showed an empty triangle. On the striped shirt, the triangle had a bold cross through it, like a tiny no-entry sign.

"That one's crossed out," Sydney said, leaning over his shoulder. "That means no bleach."

"So the empty one means bleach is okay?" Gabriel asked. He checked the white towel's label. Empty triangle. He checked the sweatpants again. Empty triangle. Every single thing that had ever gone in the bleach load had the plain triangle, and the striped shirt had the crossed one. That was a pattern, and patterns meant something.

He set the striped shirt aside, washed the towels with bleach, and ran the lights in plain detergent. When the loads finished, he folded everything into squares that were only slightly crooked, and hung the striped shirt in the sun by the window because the internet said sunlight brightens whites. By afternoon the stripes looked whiter, though the shirt still carried a faint smell like a damp fungus from the basement, so he washed it a second time.

When his mother called that night, Gabriel held up the phone to show her the folded stacks. "Look," he said. "The striped one's clean and the towels are bright. And I learned the triangle code."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The first food bank, St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, was started in 1967 by John van Hengel.
story:
Natalie pushed the cart of canned beans down the basement hallway of the public library, where the food bank had its shelves. She had volunteered once a week for a whole month now, and she had learned the system: pasta on the left, soup in the middle, cereal up top. Ms. Sharma, the librarian who ran the whole thing, had one rule that seemed completely arbitrary to Natalie, that every last can of soup had to face label-forward, even the dented ones. "It makes the shelves look full," Ms. Sharma had said. "People deserve full."

The problem started on a Tuesday, when Natalie counted the oatmeal canisters and came up three short. She had counted them herself on Saturday. Nobody had signed out any boxes since then. On Thursday, four more canisters were gone, and a bag of rice too, and still the sign-out sheet stayed blank. She told Ariella, who shelved books upstairs between visits. "That's weird," Ariella said. "But my mom says when stuff disappears at the pool, it's usually the staff, not the swimmers."

Natalie didn't want to believe that. It would imply that Ms. Sharma, who arranged story hour and taped up posters about kindness, was walking food out the side door. But the pattern pointed somewhere. The missing food was always the same kind: quick, kid-friendly stuff, oatmeal and rice and macaroni. Nobody steals randomly like that, Natalie thought. Random would be soup and beans too. Someone was choosing.

On Saturday she came early, before the library opened, and sat on the stairs with a granola bar, watching the side door through the railings. The basement was dim. Somewhere a heater ticked. She waited so long her legs went numb, and she was about to give up when the door opened and Ms. Sharma came through it, carrying two canvas bags, heavy ones, handles stretched tight. Natalie's stomach dropped. She followed, quietly, up the ramp and past the returns desk, and out into the morning.

Ms. Sharma didn't get in a car. She walked three blocks to a house with a folded wheelchair ramp and knocked, and a boy from Natalie's grade, the one who had been out sick for weeks, opened the door. His arm was in a cast from a bad cut that had gotten infected, and his mother was working doubles. Ms. Sharma handed over the bags and said, "I didn't put it on the sheet because it's nobody's business."

Back in the break room later, Natalie stared at the poster on the wall while she ate her lunch. She had read it a hundred times but never really looked: the first food bank was St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, started in 1967 by a man named John van Hengel. One person, one city, and now there were shelves of food in a library basement in a town he'd never seen.

She got up, found Ms. Sharma, and said, "The oatmeal. I know. I won't write it down either." Ms. Sharma looked at her for a long moment. "Then grab a cart," she said, "because we're three blocks short on Tuesday."

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: French uses the verb "avoir" (to have) to give age: "J'ai douze ans" means "I am twelve," but word for word says "I have twelve years."
story:
The bakery smelled like warm butter, and Zoey stood at the counter trying to remember every French word her family had crammed on the plane. Her mother wanted a baguette, her father wanted coffee, and Zoey wanted to order by herself, in French, without her voice going all volatile and squeaky the way it did when she was nervous.

The baker asked her something that ended in "âge?" and Zoey understood enough to know he was asking how old she was. She had prepared for this. Sort of. "Je suis douze ans," she said, proud of herself, because je suis meant I am and douze meant twelve. The baker shook his head, so she tried again, louder, as if volume were the problem. Behind her in the line, a boy about her age cleared his throat.

"J'ai douze ans," he said. His name turned out to be Gregoire, and his English was better than her French by roughly the ratio of a lake to a puddle. "In French, you say I have twelve years. J'ai, not je suis."

"But in English it's I am twelve," Zoey said, and then she stopped, because she could feel the shape of a rule hiding underneath the difference, something she couldn't see directly but could test. "So what about my family? I have a sister. J'ai une soeur?" Gregoire nodded. "And I have a dog. J'ai un chien?" He nodded again, and Zoey grinned so wide the baker laughed. "So you use avoir for everything you have, and that includes your years. Your age is a thing you own."

They moved to a small table by the window while the coffee brewed. Gregoire pointed at a family photo on the wall, three generations of bakers, and Zoey tried to depict them in full sentences: "Il a soixante ans. Elle a un chien blanc. Ils ont quatre enfants." Each one came out a little smoother than the last. When she stumbled, she wrote the phrase in her notebook, the one her teacher Mr. Qureshi had told her to carry everywhere, and when her parents finally claimed their coffee, her page was nearly full.

"Il a un chat," Gregoire said suddenly, pointing at the doorway, where an orange cat had wandered in and settled on a flour sack like it paid rent.

Zoey laughed. "Il a neuf ans," she said, "et il a beaucoup de pain." The cat blinked at her, completely unbothered, and the baker slid a free croissant across the counter.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Blocking is rejecting or ignoring a partner's offer, such as saying 'we're not on a boat', and it usually stops the scene from moving forward.
story:
Jacob stood in the wings of the community theatre, holding a rubber chicken like it was a gold trophy. Mr. Popal's improv workshop had seemed easy when Jacob signed up with Callan and John, but now the stage looked enormous under the lights.

"All you do," Mr. Popal announced, "is take the stage with a partner and build a scene. Ready? Jacob and Callan, you're up."

Callan began brilliantly. He gripped an invisible wheel and shouted, "Look out, Captain, a storm's coming and the cargo's sliding!"

Jacob's mind went white. "What cargo? We're not on a boat," he said. "We're in the kitchen."

The audience went quiet. Callan's hands dropped from the wheel, and he stood there with nothing to say, because there was no wheel and no storm and no kitchen either, really. After five endless seconds, Mr. Popal called time. Jacob jogged offstage feeling like he'd knocked over a birthday cake.

"That was blocking," Callan said as they sat on the steps by the prop table. "You said no to the boat."

"I panicked," Jacob admitted. But his brain was already turning. So the scene had died because he'd rejected Callan's offer. If he'd said yes instead, and added something, the scene would have kept rolling. It was like a rule hiding under the game, invisible until you broke it. He turned the idea over, testing it against what he'd watched. When John and a girl had done a bit about selling a haunted toaster, they'd both said yes to everything, even the ghost, and the audience had laughed until the girl snorted. Nobody had gone quiet then.

"I want to try again," Jacob told Mr. Popal at the break. "With John."

Mr. Popal raised an eyebrow. "Bold. Fine."

This time John started. "Sir, I regret to inform you that you have not paid your mortgage, and the bank is sending me, a bank wizard, to collect."

Jacob almost laughed. His whole body wanted to say, that's ridiculous, there's no such thing as a bank wizard. Instead he grabbed an imaginary letter from John's outstretched hand. "I see. Then I shall pay you in enchanted coins, each one worth a thousand mortgages." He elaborated on the spot, stacking invisible coin after coin into John's arms until John staggered under the pretend weight.

"The coins are floating!" John cried. "The bank wizard's spell has gone wrong!"

"Then we're both rich and falling upward," Jacob declared, and the audience roared.

When they came offstage, Callan punched his shoulder. "See? Yes, and."

Jacob grinned and looked back at the lit stage, where Mr. Popal was already waving them over. "That," Jacob said, "was ironic. The best scene of my life was about a mortgage."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: Copying =SUM(B2:B10) one column to the right turns it into =SUM(C2:C10), because ordinary cell references are relative and shift with the formula.
story:
Declan's mother had one rule for bring-your-kid-to-work day: stay out of the way. He was doing fine at that until the office printer jammed, and then, while he waited for the repairman, he noticed her screen.

She had a spreadsheet full of numbers, a column of sales for every week of the quarter, and she was adding them by hand. On a calculator. He watched her type a number, press plus, type another, press plus again, all the way down column B, and his fingers itched.

"You know the computer can do that," he said.

"It can?"

"Vihaan showed me once. There's a formula." He leaned over her keyboard, typed =SUM(B2:B10) into the empty cell under her numbers, and pressed Enter. The total appeared instantly, and his mother laughed out loud. "Declan, do you know how many hours I've spent on that calculator?"

He felt tall as anything. Then she ruined it by pointing at the next column over. "Can you do that one too?"

Column C. Then column D. Then E, F and G, all the way across the quarter. Eleven more columns, and he only knew one formula. He remembered Vihaan saying something once about the formula knowing where it was, but he couldn't recall the details, and the repairman was still wrestling with the printer behind them, so Vihaan couldn't be messaged quietly. He tried typing =SUM(B2:B10) into the cell under column C and the total was wrong. Too small. The spreadsheet was totaling column B again, sitting under column C like a liar.

That's when he thought of the copy command. Vihaan had said the formula shifts when it moves. Declan didn't trust it, though. A formula was invisible; you couldn't watch it change the way you could watch a printer repairman yank a crumpled page free. So he decided to test it in a place where it couldn't hurt anything. He copied the cell from under column B, clicked the empty cell under column C, pasted, and clicked into the cell to look.

The formula had changed by itself. It read =SUM(C2:C10). He checked the total against the column above it and it matched. He pasted the same copied cell across the whole row, under every column, and one by one, every week's total appeared, correct, like the spreadsheet was reading his mind.

Later, when the repairman left and Mr. De Vries from the next desk came over to see what the commotion was, Declan showed him the whole trick, the formula, the copy, the chart he'd built from the totals with blue bars for every week. Mr. De Vries was quiet for a moment.

"Could you do that to my numbers?" he asked, pulling out his chair. "They're in a monstrous file. It might compress my week from two days to about ten minutes."

Declan rolled Mr. De Vries's chair over, sat down, and typed.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Subtracting an element's atomic number from an atom's mass number gives the number of neutrons, because the mass number counts protons plus neutrons.
story:
John flattened the wrinkled poster against the gymnasium table and weighed its corners down with beakers he wasn't supposed to touch. The periodic table printed across it had smudged in his backpack, and three atomic numbers had turned into gray blobs. His whole project, the one that was supposed to save him from a failing grade in science, depended on those numbers.

"You're still fixing that?" Cleo whispered from the next table, where her volcano sat polished and perfect. She wanted the blue ribbon so badly she had practiced her speech on the bus twice that morning. "Judging starts in ten minutes, John."

"I know," he said. He had written quiz questions for the judges, and the third one was ruined. The question asked how many neutrons a certain atom had, and the answer had to come from the poster, but the atomic number had vanished into a smudge. He stared at the grid of squares. He knew the mass number for his element, carbon, sat at the top of the box, a twelve. He had copied that part down last night at his grandmother's kitchen table, along with something she had read aloud from her old textbook: the atomic number counts protons.

A judge in a gray sweater was already drifting toward Cleo's table. Ms. Tran, his science teacher, stood near the door, watching him the way she did when she expected him to quit. John wiped his palms on his jeans. His practice sheet from last night was folded in his pocket, and he pulled it out, hoping the missing number was somewhere in his own handwriting. It wasn't. There was only the twelve, and next to it, the number of protons he'd worked out then, six, because the atomic number was six.

He stopped. Six protons, twelve for the mass number. He mouthed the math. Twelve take away six. If the mass number counted protons plus neutrons, then whatever was left over had to be the neutrons. His pencil hovered. Six. He tested the idea on another element from memory, oxygen, mass number sixteen, atomic number eight, and again the leftover made sense: eight neutrons. It wasn't random guessing; it worked twice, the same rule both times, like a pattern hiding behind the numbers.

"Next table," the judge called, and suddenly he was standing in front of John.

John pointed at the smudged square. "Carbon has six protons," he said, "and its mass number is twelve, so subtracting the atomic number from the mass number gives six neutrons." The judge raised an eyebrow, wrote something on her clipboard, and slid the sheet aside. "Show me on another element," she said.

John's finger moved down the poster and stopped on nitrogen. "Fifteen minus seven."
